reviewed: CODEX_MASTER_PROMPT.md v1.0 (3151 lines), 00_README.md, research-data/infra/infra_facts_tooling.json, infra_facts_services.json (gh, Telegram facts), myoassist_facts.json, probe/results_2026-09-23/{gpu_probe_2026-09-23.json, compose_report.json, compose_models.py, env.sh, pip_list.txt}, smat_spec.json (targeted)

findings.where: Part N.9 steps 1-8; N.3 reissue registry; N.5 loop (the bridge owns expiries and reissues); E.4 Phase 0 (up to 2 h) and E.8 step 5; 00_README 'How to start'
findings.problem: Every user-dependent M0 step is serial behind the GitHub login: login -> repository -> Pages -> drop page -> bot token -> bridge. Between N.9 step 3 and step 6, no process owns the device-code reissue, the polling of issues for the secret drop, or starting the bridge. Reissue lives in bridge/reissue.py, but the bridge starts only at step 6, and the wrapper is installed and armed only at step 8. Phase 0 (up to 2 h: reading about 95 pages, probes, codex exec canaries, PLAN.md, the first commit) also runs before need 1, while E.8 and the README promise the code 'within the first hour'. During the DGIST-bot phase messages carry no buttons, so after the 3 automatic reissues (about 1 h) the user has no way to ask for a new code.
findings.scenario: The user pastes the first message and leaves. About 1.5 h later need 1 arrives through the DGIST bot, and three codes expire unread over the next hour. The first session builds the bridge and the wrapper against the fake backend and then has nothing independent left, because steps 4-8 all need the repository, so under E.4(a) it ends with its report. Nothing is running that can reissue a code, read the drop issue or start the bridge, and the wrapper is not armed. The build is dead until the user walks back to the PC, which is the forge failure N.1 was written to prevent. Keeping the session alive to poll instead would break 'Codex never waits'.
findings.fix: (1) E.8: insert step 0 before reading the full prompt: 'Start the GitHub device flow (N.7 command) in a transient unit, print the code in this session and send it through the DGIST bot (send-only). The user has just pasted the first message and is at the PC.' 00_README 'How to start', add: 'Stay about 30 minutes with your phone: you will get a GitHub code, then a request to create the bot.' (2) N.9: replace steps 2-8 with: 'Before anything else in M0, build and enable smatsprint-bootstrap.service (stdlib only, ctl slice, Restart=always). It owns device-code reissue in the DGIST phase: a fresh code when the last one has expired, at most one every 2 h between 08:00 and 23:00 KST, for 72 h, then one PC-fallback message. Once gh_auth passes it runs the scripted, fake-tested repository and Pages creation of step 4, polls the drop issues every 60 s, applies the bot token, checks getMe and /start, starts smatsprint-bridge, and arms the wrapper for an M0-finish session (canaries, real-bot smoke, the builder-mode need if still unset). The first session may end as soon as this unit is installed and its fake-backend tests pass.' (3) Keep in Phase 0 only the one-command probes. Move the EGL render and the jailed CUDA probe to a detached job that does not delay need 1.
findings.test: Rehearsal with fake GitHub and fake Telegram: the user completes the login 5 h after the start, and the first Codex session ended at 2 h. Assert that the bootstrap unit alone reissues codes within the policy, creates the repository and Pages, applies the drop, starts the bridge, and that the wrapper then launches exactly one M0-finish session. On the real start, assert that need 1 is created within 10 minutes of the first session starting (state/needs/events.jsonl timestamp).

findings.where: Part N.8 'Builder mode' (options 1 and 2; 'Until the user answers, sessions do CPU-only work'); N.9 (no step sends the decision); 00_README Defaults 'Builder mode' and Question 1
findings.problem: The flags the wrapper uses are defined only 'once the user taps' option 1 or 2. N.8 says 'Until the user answers, sessions do CPU-only work', but gives no flags for those sessions, and no sandboxed mode can do that work. In workspace-write, .git is read-only (fact codex-31), so even local commits fail, and network is off by default (codex-30), so uv sync cannot install. The decision is a pick_one need with buttons, so it can be answered only after the programme's own bot and bridge exist (N.9 step 6). Yet N.9 never lists sending it, and nothing says whether it has blocks_build.
findings.scenario: At the end of M0 the wrapper is armed with no mode. It may launch M1 with guessed flags: bypass without the user's consent, or a sandboxed mode in which every commit, uv sync and systemctl --user call fails, giving three quick failures, BACKOFF and then build_stuck. Or it holds M1 indefinitely because Codex marked the need blocks_build. Whether the build proceeds, stalls or runs unguarded depends on Codex's guess.
findings.fix: (1) 00_README 'How to start', step 2: append to the pasted message the line 'Builder mode: 1' (full access with guardrails) or 'Builder mode: 2' (auto-review). In Defaults write: 'Builder mode: asked in the first message, while you are at the PC. Only if you leave it out does it become a phone need.' (2) N.8: replace 'Until the user answers, sessions do CPU-only work that needs neither pushing nor the GPU, and queue the rest.' with 'The wrapper never launches a session while builder_mode is unset. If the first message did not set it, the decision need is sent right after the bridge starts (N.9 step 6a), with blocks_build: true, reply pick_one and no default. The M0 report says the build waits on this one tap.' (3) N.9: insert step 6a with that need. (4) Record the chosen mode in state/codexwrap/state.json and docs/PLAN.md.
findings.test: Wrapper unit test: with builder_mode unset, it stays in HOLD(builder_mode) and launches nothing. Setting the mode through the fake bridge launches exactly one session whose recorded command line contains exactly that mode's flags. A grep test asserts that no code path launches codex exec without reading builder_mode.

findings.where: Part N.8 'The session command' ('in smatsprint-ctl.slice with CPU and memory caps'); Part R.2 host-resource fence (smatsprint-ctl.slice CPUQuota=200%, MemoryMax=1G); E.4 detach.sh (no slice named); H.4 layer 4 (writes from the ctl slice are not flagged)
findings.problem: Wrapper-launched Codex sessions run inside smatsprint-ctl.slice, which R.2 caps at 2 CPUs and 1 GB in total, shared with the controller, runner, bridge, wrapper and watchdog. A child cgroup cannot exceed its parent, so per-session caps change nothing. A build session must run uv sync, pytest with torch imported (about 0.5-1 GB), load the composed model (560 MB when loaded from XML per the probe), run trainer smoke tests with 32 env processes, and run the crash matrix. detach.sh names no slice. And because writes from the ctl slice are exempt from the out-of-band detector, an unattended builder's writes to ledger/, a frozen gate/ or a frozen eval/ are never flagged.
findings.scenario: The first unattended session (M1) runs out of memory inside the 1 GB slice on its first test run. The cgroup OOM killer may pick the runner or the controller instead of pytest. From M2 on, while the campaign runs, this can kill the controller mid-pause or stall the bridge. CPU-bound tests crawl at 200 %. Codex either keeps failing, ending in build_stuck, or rewrites slice properties that the prompt calls the user's split.
findings.fix: R.2: add a slice and a unit row. 'smatsprint-build.slice (top level, not a child of smatsprint.slice): CPUQuota=800%, MemoryHigh=5G, MemoryMax=6G, MemorySwapMax=0, TasksMax=2048. Codex build sessions and every detach.sh job run there. A detach.sh job marked --heavy or --gpu-work runs in smatsprint-exp.slice as a job of class build: the worker's packer admits it under the same host-RAM rule (MemAvailable minus declared RAM > 6 GB) and within the exp CPU quota.' N.8: replace 'in smatsprint-ctl.slice with CPU and memory caps' with 'in smatsprint-build.slice'. H.4 layer 4: 'Build sessions are not exempt. Their writes to ledger/, record/, state/, queue/, work/, configs/registered/ or a frozen gate/ or eval/ are flagged like any other out-of-band write (see IM-15).' The ctl slice keeps 1 GB for the four services only.
findings.test: Integration: a fake session in the build slice allocates 5 GB and spawns 16 busy processes. Assert that the controller, runner, bridge and wrapper stay alive, that heartbeats continue, and that /pause completes within 90 s during the load. `systemctl --user show smatsprint-codex-1 -p Slice` returns smatsprint-build.slice.

findings.where: Part N.8 'Launch rule', 'When a session ends' and 'Failures'; E.4 end conditions (a)-(c); N.9 step 8 (the wrapper is armed from inside the interactive first session)
findings.problem: The launch rule checks only blocking needs, the build-pause button and the usage-limit cool-down. A session may end under E.4(b) ('everything left depends on a detached job with more than ten minutes to run'), or under (a) without marking a need blocks_build. The wrapper then goes to ARMED(next) and relaunches at once. The next session finds the same detached job, ends cleanly within minutes, and the loop repeats. A clean quick exit is not a 'failure', so BACKOFF never triggers, and HOLD depends on parsing free text ('if the report names a blocker'). Separately, N.9 step 8 arms the wrapper from inside the interactive first session. That session is not a smatsprint-codex-* unit, so the one-session check cannot see it, and M1 can start while the first session is still committing and writing its report.
findings.scenario: M1 detaches a 3 h calibration and ends. The wrapper relaunches every few minutes. Each xhigh session re-reads AGENTS.md, PROGRESS.md and the governing Part (tens of thousands of tokens) and exits. That is dozens of sessions and on the order of a million tokens or more, drawn from the Codex quota the forge's builder shares on the same account. At the end of M0, two builders edit /home/aurnab/projects/smat-sprint at the same time.
findings.fix: N.8 'Launch rule', add three conditions. '(d) No detached job listed in the last session's outcome as waited_on is still running; its exit (state/detached/<name>/exit_code) re-arms the wrapper. (e) Every session is launched with --output-schema ops/codexwrap/outcome.schema.json, whose final JSON is {milestone, milestone_complete, end_reason: a|b|c, waited_on_detached: [...], blocking_need_ids: [...], report_md}. If end_reason is a and no blocks_build need is open, or if two consecutive sessions produced no commit and no new need, the wrapper goes to HOLD and raises build_stuck. (f) Never launch within 10 minutes of the previous session's end.' N.9 step 8: 'The interactive first session writes state/codexwrap/sessions/0/{last_message.md, ended_at} and, as its very last action, removes state/codexwrap/interactive.lock (created at its start). The wrapper launches nothing while interactive.lock exists and is younger than 12 h.'
findings.test: Wrapper unit tests with a fake codex. A session ending with end_reason b and a 30-minute fake detached job produces zero launches until exit_code appears, then exactly one. end_reason a with no blocking need gives HOLD, not a launch. With interactive.lock present, arming launches nothing. Over a simulated 24 h, the launch count never exceeds the number of distinct wake events.

findings.where: Part E.4 M1 list and exit; B.7 intro ('At the end of M1 the runner registers these blocks ... fully pre-registered'); B.6 positive control P1; Part G ('gate/ complete for every path'); C.9 (one EVAL_HASH over every protocol); E.4 'The machine does science from the first day of M1'; E.4 M0 exit ('the /pause command before any job runs')
findings.problem: Before the first registered experiment, M1 must deliver: the environment; the trainer; eval/ for every protocol (walk, sprint, parity, partner transfer, offline replay); gate/ for L0-L5 and all three paper paths, with synthetic-ledger suites; the runner, worker and controller; the out-of-band watcher; cards; and every Q0-Q7 config fully registered. That registration drags in all of B.6: B0-B5, A1-A4, K1 and cross-play; the B4 profile, digitised from the published figure or chosen; and the Molinaro walking dataset, a held-out asset 'reserved in M1'. Because Q2 samples registry choice 5, it also needs the external reference dataset and the phase-matched option. It also needs P1, which runs our env and trainer on MyoAssist's 22-muscle tutorial config, so walk26 must support a second, planar, 22-muscle model with a different (ankle) device. E.4 asks for early detached Stage-1 runs 'under the sprintctl pause that M1 provides', but the M1 list builds the controller and pause after the env, trainer, eval and gate. M0 already tells the user about /pause, before any controller exists.
findings.scenario: M1 runs many 10 h sessions of infrastructure before the first Q2 job, which is A.2's 'no training run for weeks' again. The alternative is detached pre-ledger runs that cannot be paused from the phone, and whose outcomes Codex sees before it writes Q2's space and selection rule, which weakens the pre-registration.
findings.fix: E.4: split M1. 'M1a (target 1-2 sessions): first the pause path. That means the exp slice, the worker unit, and the LAB-only subset of the D.2 state machine written as the pure function (pause, resume, stop, drain, emergency_stop, polite pause, job delivery, record copier), plus sprintctl pause|resume|status and bridge /pause. Then walk26 on the native backend with the MyoAssist reference and h3d_default/h3d_phase; the trainer with its correctness tests; eval/core and walk_eval for the L0-L2 metrics; gate L0-L2; the runner, ledger, registration and queue. Then register and start Q0, Q1 (throughput only) and Q2 restricted to registry choices 1, 2, 6, 7 and 8. M1b (while Q2 runs): stages S2-S4, the B.6 controls, gate L3-L4 and the walking paper paths, and the S4, offline-replay and partner-transfer protocols. Register Q3-Q7 before the first S2 checkpoint exists. Deferred without loss of integrity: the out-of-band watcher (M3, when the sandbox exists; hash checks at job start and the hash chains cover M1-M2); the card validator (M2); P1 (register it before any Q4 result, since it is needed only before a negative verdict); the external-reference and phase-matched options (a later sweep); the Phase-2 gate and eval (their own hash family, frozen before the first sprint result; see IM-13); the MyoAssist trainer cross-check (optional).' Add: 'Runs started before the ledger exists are plumbing and throughput only. Their outcomes are not used to choose Q2's space or rule.'
findings.test: Acceptance line: the first registered Q2 stage_train job starts within 24 h of the first M1 session starting. ledger/candidates.jsonl shows Q3-Q7 registered before any S2 checkpoint exists (compare timestamps). `sprintctl pause` and /pause stop every smatsprint-exp.slice process before the first job of any kind starts.

findings.where: Part E.2 Integration and Crash groups; E.4 M1 exit; R.2 cold-start drill ('network faked down for 60 s'); C.8 and E.2 'Trainer correctness'
findings.problem: The M1 exit, and so the campaign start, waits on long wall-clock suites: two 10-minute 'stays inactive' holds; 100 real pause/resume cycles, each up to about 50 s to stop plus up to 120 s for the heartbeat; 50 SIGKILL moments, each compared with a never-killed twin; runner kills during harvest, planning and git commit; and the cold-start drill. Together that is several hours. The prompt does not say which slice or admission these tests use. 'Network faked down' has no user-space mechanism, because a network namespace would need root. 'A standard continuous-control task ... reaches the return band of a reference implementation within a fixed budget' names no task, band or budget.
findings.scenario: Codex runs the suites in the foreground or in the session slice (IM-03), serialises them, and holds the campaign for most of a day. Or it improvises an OS-level network cut. Or it picks an arbitrary PPO benchmark and band, then tunes until the test passes.
findings.fix: E.4 M1 exit: 'Campaign-start gate: the Unit, Gate and Trainer groups; L0; one real pause/resume cycle with the GPU and CPU verified free; one SIGKILL-resume bit-equality check. The full Integration and Crash groups and the cold-start drill then run detached in smatsprint-exp.slice as build-class jobs while the campaign runs. Any red result puts the programme in SAFE_PAUSE and raises unexpected.' R.2: 'Network faked down means the service adapters (Git, Telegram, Vast, Drive) run with SMATSPRINT_FAULT=offline:60, which makes every call raise Unreachable. No OS-level network change.' C.8: 'Trainer correctness task: Gymnasium HalfCheetah-v5, 1 M steps, 3 seeds. The band is CleanRL ppo_continuous_action's published mean return at 1 M steps minus 2 SD, recorded in tests/fixtures/ppo_band.json. gymnasium goes in the dev dependency group, not the science lock (IM-12).'
findings.test: Less than 30 minutes pass between the campaign-start gate going green and the first Q0 job starting. A deliberately failing crash test injected into the detached suite puts the running campaign in SAFE_PAUSE within 2 minutes.

findings.where: Part B.2 'Body and device' and 'Stage 1 without the device'; A.4 (previous sprint venv, read-only); B.5 probe facts; C.2 uv.lock; probe compose_report.json and compose_models.py
findings.problem: B.2 says to compose with compose_env_model(..., planar_root=True) but never says in which environment. The probe composed in the old, read-only sprint venv (MuJoCo 3.4.0, assist_sim 1.0.0, myo_sim 0.2.2) with a free root (nq 47), then simulated the model in a fresh MuJoCo 3.14.0 venv. So B.2's 'facts of the composed model', and every RSS and throughput number, describe the free-root model, not the planar-root model (nq = nv = 46) the prompt mandates. Putting assist_sim, myo_sim or MyoSuite into the new lock may conflict with mujoco 3.14.0, because MyoSuite releases have pinned MuJoCo exactly. .mjb files are also specific to the MuJoCo version. The probe's human-only compose monkeypatches load_combined and ignores planar_root, so the bare planar-root comparator that the Stage-1 identity test needs does not exist yet. Finally, stage edits applied at runtime (gain, zero device mass, contype, timestep) change the model without changing any file hash.
findings.scenario: Codex adds assist_sim and MyoSuite to the M1 lock, the resolver pins MuJoCo below 3.14, and M4's Warp track later forces a version change, so the code_id and the model change mid-campaign. Or Codex composes and saves the .mjb in the old venv, and the runtime cannot load it. Or the ledger records a file hash that does not identify the model that was actually simulated.
findings.fix: B.2, add: 'Composition runs once, read-only, in the previous sprint venv (PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1, with cwd, TMPDIR and caches under <project>/cache), exactly as research-data/probe/results_2026-09-23/compose_models.py did, with planar_root=True, and exports self-contained XML plus assets. Our <option> element (integrator, solver, iterations, cone, <flag multiccd="disable"/>) is added to the exported XML. The .mjb is compiled and saved in the pinned runtime venv (mujoco==3.14.0, with mujoco-warp and warp-lang pinned in the science lock from M1), and is regenerated whenever the pinned MuJoCo changes. The runtime depends only on mujoco: no assist_sim, myo_sim or myosuite in the science lock. Stage edits (gainprm; device body mass and inertia set to 0, followed by mj_setConst; geom contype and conaffinity; opt.timestep) are applied to the loaded MjModel. The model hash in every row is the sha256 of mj_saveModel of that effective model. Q1 re-measures the model facts and the throughput on the planar-root model. Stage-1 identity test: compare against a bare myolegs26 composed by the same pipeline plus assist_sim.root_frame.to_planar_root. If that cannot be produced, run the 300-step identity test on the free-root exports (human vs massless human_plus_hippo), which the probe showed compose reproducibly.'
findings.test: Loading the .mjb in the runtime venv gives nq = nv = 46, the six root joint names, MULTICCD disabled and the recorded MuJoCo version. `uv tree --only-group science` lists no myosuite, assist_sim or myo_sim. The effective-model hash differs between the Stage-2 and Stage-3 configs and is stable across two loads. The massless-device identity test passes with max |qpos difference| = 0 over 300 steps.

findings.where: Part C.8 trainer; C.11; R.2 'Thread caps' ('the trainer process uses at most 4 threads'); C.4 resource classes; B.7 time estimates ('about 20,000 end-to-end transitions per second')
findings.problem: The prompt never says whether the PPO update of CPU-physics jobs runs on the GPU or the CPU. R.2's 4-thread trainer cap implies the CPU. SMAT's update is 20 epochs over 65,536 samples in minibatches of 16,384, on a model of about 140k parameters: roughly 1 TFLOP per update. On 4 CPU threads that takes roughly 4-11 s, against about 3 s to collect 65,536 transitions with 32 envs at 1/1200 s physics (probe: about 2,050 transitions/s per thread at 10 substeps). The end-to-end rate would therefore be about 5-10k transitions/s, not the 20k/s B.7 assumes, and the env pool would idle during every update. The same choice decides whether Phase-1 jobs hold the GPU, and so whether polite pause and the GPU-free check matter for the campaign at all, and whether results need a learner-device field for comparability.
findings.scenario: Codex picks the CPU learner: Q2 takes 2-4 times longer than 'about 4 days', and the dashboard ETAs are wrong. Or it picks the GPU learner without saying so: every job becomes a GPU job under admission, polite-pause and backend-class rules that were not written for that.
findings.fix: C.8, add: 'The PPO update runs on the GPU (CUDA) by default for every job; the physics backend is unchanged. Resource class cpu_env+gpu_learner declares about 1 GB of VRAM per job. A CPU learner (4 threads) is a registered alternative, used only when the GPU is unavailable. Rows record learner_device. Runs that differ only in learner_device are comparable within the tolerance the Q1 cross-check measures.' B.7 Q1: 'Measure end-to-end transitions/s at 32 envs for both learners, and recompute every B.7 time before Q2 is registered.'
findings.test: Q1's throughput row reports both learner devices. A unit test asserts that the default job spec has learner_device=cuda and that polite pause stops such jobs. The Q2 ETA on the dashboard comes from the measured rate, not the constant 20,000.

findings.where: Part C.7 'Calibrated tiers' ('it is part of the pre-loaded campaign, Part B.7 Q1') vs the B.7 table row Q1 ('~100 M', '~2 h'); C.7 evaluation noise floor; B.7 Q1 'evaluation noise floor'; G.4 precision rule
findings.problem: C.7 puts the tier calibration in Q1: at least 8 configurations, each at P1 (40 M) and P3 (320 M), on 2 seeds. That is about 5.8 B transitions, as much as Q2 itself and roughly 3 days at 20k/s. B.7 budgets Q1 at about 100 M and 2 h. Q1 also lists 'evaluation noise floor', but the noise of symmetry r, toe-off, speed and fall rate is undefined for policies that fall within 1-2 control steps. The probe found zero-action episodes end after 1-2 steps, and G.3 rejects cycles shorter than 0.6 s. No walking checkpoint exists at Q1.
findings.scenario: Codex either runs a 5.8 B calibration before Q2, delaying the Stage-1 search by about 3 days, or skips it and violates C.7 ('Before a sweep's P1 selection is trusted ... the tier calibration ... must exist'). The Q1 noise-floor job produces NaN or meaningless floors, and C.7's 'too close to call' rule is then built on them.
findings.fix: B.7 Q1 row: 'CPU throughput table only (8, 16, 32, 48 env processes; RSS; transitions/s for both learners; IM-08); ~0.1 B; ~2 h.' C.7: replace 'it is part of the pre-loaded campaign, Part B.7 Q1' with: 'It is part of Q2. Before Q2 starts, 8 of its 24 P1 configurations, drawn by sha256(sweep_id), also run at P3 on 2 seeds; the 3 miss-check members count toward the 8. Q2's rule uses P1 only if the calibration passes, otherwise P2, as declared at registration.' G.4 and C.7: 'The evaluation noise floor is a registered calibration job, run on the first checkpoint that meets L1, and again on the first S2 and S4 checkpoints before any S4 claim.'
findings.test: campaign.yaml validates with a Q1 budget of at most 0.15 B. Q2's registration names its calibration members and its fallback tier. The job schema refuses a noise-floor job whose checkpoint has not met L1.

findings.where: Part G.5 held-out assets ('No search, sweep, sandbox run or tuning job may touch them (the job schema rejects it...)'); C.3 Seeds; C.10 Seeds ('evaluation never uses a training seed or a sandbox seed'); B.7 Q2 selection rule; B.6 B3 ('tuned on training seeds')
findings.problem: Q2 selects configs by the L1 criteria, which need evaluation episodes. Yet no pool is legal for sweep or tuning evaluation: the evaluation pool (10,000-10,999) is a held-out asset the job schema must reject for sweep jobs, C.10 forbids evaluating on training seeds, and the sandbox pool belongs to the sandbox. B3's 'tuned on training seeds' contradicts C.10. Separately, the training-seed universe 0-999 contains the reserved partner seeds 900-949, while C.3 demands a unit test proving the pools are disjoint.
findings.scenario: Implemented literally, the schema rejects Q2's P1 eval jobs and the Stage-1 search can select nothing. Or Codex quietly evaluates sweep members on the held-out pool, which is exactly what G.5 forbids. Or a candidate's sha256 draw hands it a partner seed, and the disjointness test fails or gets weakened.
findings.fix: C.3 Seeds: 'Training seeds are drawn from 0-899; partner seeds 900-949 are reserved and never drawn. Validation seeds 30,000-30,999 are used by every sweep's selection rule, controller tuning (the B3 and B4 grids), the precision-rule noise measurement and the proxy-tier calibration. Evaluation seeds 10,000-10,999 are used only for claim evaluations and final reporting.' G.5 and C.10: add the validation pool, and state that sweep and tuning jobs must use it and are rejected on the evaluation pool.
findings.test: eval/core/seeds.py tests: all five pools are pairwise disjoint. A sweep member's eval job on the 10,000 pool is rejected, and on the 30,000 pool accepted. A property test over 10,000 random candidate ids never draws a seed in 900-949.

findings.where: Part G.4 'Precision rule'; C.9 walking protocol ('the episode count E is raised, never the band'); C.9 EVAL_HASH; R.10 ('Change gate/, eval/ or a tolerance'); G.8 (changes only through sprintctl over SSH)
findings.problem: G.4 has 'the runner' raise the evaluation episode count E automatically when measured noise exceeds a quarter of a band half-width, but the prompt never says where E lives. If E is in eval/protocols, raising it changes EVAL_HASH, opens an evaluation epoch, and is an automatic change to eval/, which R.10 forbids. If E is outside the hashed trees, it becomes an unhashed evaluation parameter that anyone with settings access could change.
findings.scenario: Codex puts E in settings, which creates an unfrozen lever over every gated number. Or it puts E in eval/, and the first noise measurement opens an epoch and forces a re-evaluation of every claim checkpoint, an action the runner is forbidden to take on its own.
findings.fix: G.4, replace the mechanism of the precision rule with: 'E is computed by a frozen function in eval/protocols/walk_eval.py: E = min(200, max(20, ceil(20 * (4 * sigma_hat / h)^2))). sigma_hat is the per-metric noise from the latest registered noise-floor calibration row for that stage (a ledger row; IM-09), and h is the band half-width read from gate/criteria.yaml. Raising E therefore changes no hash and opens no epoch. Every eval row records E and the calibration row it came from, and a claim's E is fixed when the claim is created.'
findings.test: Unit test: a synthetic noise row doubles E for the same checkpoint while EVAL_HASH and GATE_HASH stay unchanged. A settings command that tries to set E is rejected by the schema. A claim created before a new noise row keeps its E.

findings.where: Part C.2 ('code_id is the sha256 of the git tree hashes of smatsprint/, eval/ and uv.lock'); C.10 'the same code identity'; R.9; B.5 (Warp added in M4); E.2 job-identity test
findings.problem: The single uv.lock also receives the tooling added during M0-M7: PyNaCl, pytest, hypothesis, playwright, gymnasium for the PPO check, plus mujoco-warp and warp-lang in M4. Each addition changes code_id for every new candidate even though no science changed. Comparisons across code identities are refused ('not comparable'), and every lock hash gets its own run-tree venv.
findings.scenario: After M2 adds Playwright, every steering edit, every Promote and every new catalogue candidate runs under a new code_id and can no longer be paired with the SMAT, B0 and B2 arms registered in M1. The user's steering produces 'not comparable' everywhere, and the disk fills with one venv per lock hash (see IM-19).
findings.fix: C.2: 'Dependencies are split into uv dependency groups. The science group (torch, numpy, mujoco, mujoco-warp, warp-lang, safetensors, scipy, ...) is fully pinned in M1, the Warp packages included. The dev and ops groups hold everything else. code_id = sha256(tree(smatsprint/), tree(eval/), sha256(output of `uv export --frozen --only-group science --no-hashes`)). Run-tree venvs are keyed by that export hash and built with `uv sync --frozen --only-group science --no-install-project`.' E.2, add to the job-identity unit test: 'adding a dev dependency leaves code_id unchanged'.
findings.test: Add pytest-xdist to the dev group and commit: code_id is unchanged and no new run-tree venv is built. Bump numpy in the science group and commit: code_id changes.

findings.where: Part H.4 layer 3 and LI2 (a job refuses unless its eval and gate hashes equal those registered); C.9 evaluation epochs; G.8 gate epochs and `sprintctl gate-change <key> <value>`; Part G ('gate/ complete for every path' in M1); C.9 (one EVAL_HASH over all of eval/core and eval/protocols)
findings.problem: A candidate's EVAL_HASH and GATE_HASH are pinned at registration, and its jobs refuse to start on any mismatch. When an evaluation or gate epoch opens (for example after a gait-event bug fix), the prompt never says what happens to registered candidates that have not started. Under LI2 they all refuse, and the pre-loaded queue stops. One EVAL_HASH and one GATE_HASH also cover the Phase-2 sprint protocol and the L5 criteria, which cannot be written or tested against a sprint environment in M1, and adding them later is an epoch that touches every walking claim. gate-change edits keys only, so a bug in the check_gate.py code has no defined fix path.
findings.scenario: The first eval bug found in week 1 halts the whole campaign until someone re-registers dozens of candidates by hand. Or Codex writes an untestable sprint_eval.py in M1 to avoid a later epoch. Or it fixes check_gate.py in place and breaks GATE_HASH verification.
findings.fix: C.9 and G.8, add: 'Hashes are kept per family: EVAL_HASH[walk], EVAL_HASH[sprint], GATE_HASH[walk: L0-L4 and the walking paper paths], GATE_HASH[sprint: L5]. A family is frozen before the first result it judges, so the walking families freeze in M1 and the sprint families before the first sprint result. When an epoch opens, every registered candidate version with no started job is automatically re-registered as v+1 under the new epoch, with one steering row (source=epoch, the epoch's reason); paired blocks move together, and seeds and budgets are unchanged. Pipelines already started finish under their own epoch. A code fix to gate/ or eval/ goes through `sprintctl gate-release <commit> --reason` or `sprintctl eval-release <commit> --reason`, which opens an epoch, re-judges the affected claims under both epochs and shows both verdicts.'
findings.test: Open a synthetic eval epoch with 20 queued candidates: all 20 get v+1 under the new epoch within one runner cycle and start normally; running jobs are unaffected; the steering log has 20 rows with source=epoch. Adding eval/protocols/sprint_eval.py leaves EVAL_HASH[walk] unchanged.

findings.where: Part R.2 ('Each packed job runs in its own transient scope: systemd-run --user --scope --slice=smatsprint-exp.slice'; 'With KillMode=mixed ... anything still alive at TimeoutStopSec=50 is killed'; emergency stop = `systemctl --user kill --signal=SIGKILL smatsprint-worker.service`); D.2 pause and emergency_stop
findings.problem: A process started with systemd-run --scope is moved into its own scope cgroup under smatsprint-exp.slice. It is no longer in smatsprint-worker.service's cgroup. KillMode, TimeoutStopSec and `systemctl kill <service>` act only on the service's cgroup. So a packed job that ignores SIGTERM, hangs in a CUDA call or deadlocks is never killed by stopping the worker, and the emergency stop kills the worker but leaves its jobs running. The GPU-free check then fails or waits forever.
findings.scenario: A job wedged in a CUDA call keeps the GPU after Pause. The acknowledgement never comes, the 90 s promise to lab mates is broken, and 'Emergency stop' leaves 32 environment processes running.
findings.fix: R.2, replace the scope sentence and the pause and emergency lines with: 'Scopes are named smatsprint-job-<job_id>.scope and are created with -p BindsTo=smatsprint-worker.service -p After=smatsprint-worker.service. Verify on systemd 255 that transient scopes accept these properties; if they do not, the controller performs the following steps on its own. Pause: stop the worker unit; then `systemctl --user kill --signal=SIGTERM 'smatsprint-job-*.scope'`; after 45 s `systemctl --user kill --signal=SIGKILL 'smatsprint-job-*.scope'`. Pause is verified when no PID remains in smatsprint-exp.slice. Emergency stop: `systemctl --user kill --signal=SIGKILL smatsprint-worker.service 'smatsprint-job-*.scope'`, then stop both.'
findings.test: Integration: a packed dummy job traps SIGTERM and holds 1 GB of VRAM. After Pause, no PID remains in smatsprint-exp.slice within 60 s and nvidia-smi lists none of our PIDs. After an emergency stop, the same holds within 5 s.

findings.where: Part H.4 layer 4 ('A watcher (inotify on the experiment tree, plus a periodic hash sweep) attributes every write to a PID and its cgroup'); H.11 LI10; E.4 M1 list ('the out-of-band edit watcher (Part H.4 layer 4)')
findings.problem: This is not implementable in user space. inotify events carry no PID. Unprivileged fanotify (Linux 5.13 and later) allows inode marks only and does not report the PID of the writer. Attributing writes to a PID needs root: privileged fanotify, auditd or eBPF. E.5 expects no root need. The slice-based exemption also exempts the build sessions (IM-03).
findings.scenario: Codex either raises a root_needed PC trip for auditd, the one thing the README promises will not happen, or ships a watcher with fake attribution (racy /proc fd scans) that lets the LI10 'within 60 s' test pass while it cannot attribute. Either way it spends an M1 session on this before the first experiment.
findings.fix: H.4 layer 4, replace with: 'Every legitimate writer (runner, worker, controller) appends each file it creates or changes (path, size, sha256, time, component) to its own append-only write journal under state/journals/. The watcher (inotify on the experiment tree, plus a hash sweep every 10 minutes) flags any change that no journal entry explains within 60 s, showing the path, the time and "writer unknown". Attribution to a process is optional, and only with a root-installed audit rule that the user approves later.' LI10: 'Any write that no journal explains raises the flag within 60 s.' Build the watcher in M3 (IM-05).
findings.test: Fuzz: the runner writes 1,000 files with journal entries and none is flagged. A plain shell `echo >> ledger/runs.jsonl` is flagged within 60 s, and the affected jobs refuse to start. A write from the build slice to gate/ after the freeze is flagged.

findings.where: Part N.8 option 1 ('forbidden command rules in the builder's config layer for sudo, reboot, shutdown, systemctl --user stop|restart|disable on any unit not named smatsprint-*, kill of processes outside smatsprint.slice, rm -rf outside the project and sandbox trees, vastai destroy|stop without the smatsprint- label, and gh auth logout without GH_CONFIG_DIR'); fact codex-36
findings.problem: Execpolicy rules load from the rules/ directories of active config layers (fact codex-36). The user layer ~/.codex/rules/ is shared by every Codex session on the account, including the forge's builder. The project layer .codex/rules/ loads only when the project is trusted. A -p config file is not a rules directory. And prefix_rule matches argv prefixes only: it cannot express 'a unit not named smatsprint-*', 'a PID outside a slice', 'a path outside the project', 'without a label' or 'without an environment variable'.
findings.scenario: Codex writes the rules into ~/.codex/rules/. The forge's builder can then no longer `systemctl --user restart` its own clforge units, which breaks the forge. Or Codex spends a session trying to express the negations and ships a rules file that silently matches nothing, and the canary still reports 'guardrails active'.
findings.fix: N.8 option 1, replace the rule sentence with: 'Rules live only in the project, at /home/aurnab/projects/smat-sprint/.codex/rules/builder.rules. The wrapper passes -c 'projects."/home/aurnab/projects/smat-sprint".trust_level="trusted"' on the command line and never edits ~/.codex/config.toml or ~/.codex/rules/. Forbidden prefixes: sudo; reboot; shutdown; systemctl --user {stop, restart, disable, kill, mask} followed by each named foreign unit, enumerated from `systemctl --user list-unit-files` at M0 (clforge-*, dgist-*, llama-swap, open-webui, ugrp-*); vastai {create, destroy, stop, start}; gh auth logout; rm -rf /home/aurnab/projects/ugrp-cl-autoresearch. Conditions that prefix rules cannot express (PIDs outside our slice, paths outside the project, the Vast label, GH_CONFIG_DIR) are prompt rules only, and docs/PLAN.md says so.'
findings.test: M0 canary: add the forbidden prefix /home/aurnab/.local/bin/smatsprint-canary (a script that only touches state/canary/ran) to builder.rules. A bypass-mode session in the project that is asked to run it leaves no state/canary/ran. The same request with -C outside the project runs it, showing the rules are inactive elsewhere. `ls -la ~/.codex/rules` is unchanged by the build.

findings.where: Part N.8 'Builder mode' option 2 and the canary list; A.5 rule 11; facts codex-31 and codex-35
findings.problem: In option 2 the only vetted helpers are a 'git push helper' and launch-detached. But workspace-write keeps .git read-only (codex-31), so git add and git commit also fail, and the builder cannot commit at all. launch-detached takes '-- <command>', which is an arbitrary unsandboxed command and so a full escape. With network_access=true, the source reading behind codex-35 says no seccomp network filter is installed, so AF_UNIX connect to the user bus probably works inside the sandbox, and a plain systemd-run --user becomes an escape with no rule needed. The canary list tests this (`systemd-run --user --wait nvidia-smi`) but never says what a success means for the choice offered to the user. The canary `cat ~/.config/ugrp-forge/CANARY` reads inside the forge's secrets directory, which rule 11 forbids, and succeeds in both modes because neither mode restricts reads. `git push --dry-run` cannot run in Phase 0 because the repository does not exist yet.
findings.scenario: The user picks 'auto-review (more contained)'. M1 cannot commit, stalls and ends in build_stuck, and the containment was never real. The build also runs a canary that reads the forge's secrets directory.
findings.fix: N.8 option 2, replace the helper list with: 'Two vetted helpers, installed read-only in ~/.local/share/smatsprint/: smatsprint-git (add, commit and push of this repository only, through the deploy key) and launch-detached <job_id>. launch-detached accepts only a job id whose spec file, state/detached/<job_id>/spec.json, the session wrote and which validates against a fixed schema (a pytest node under tests/, a registered job kind, a declared slice). It never takes an arbitrary command.' Canaries: 'Replace `cat ~/.config/ugrp-forge/CANARY` with a canary file this programme creates outside the workspace (~/.config/smatsprint-canary/CANARY, mode 0600). Run the push canary after N.9 step 4. If `systemd-run --user --wait true` succeeds inside option 2, the decision need must say: "On this server option 2 is not contained: the sandbox can reach the systemd user bus", and recommend option 1.'
findings.test: docs/PLAN.md has one canary result line per mode per canary. A grep of the build sessions' recorded commands (state/codexwrap/sessions/*/events.jsonl) finds no access to ~/.config/ugrp-forge. In option 2, a commit through smatsprint-git succeeds, and launch-detached rejects a spec that contains an arbitrary command.

findings.where: Part A.4 Telegram ('only ever calls sendMessage on it, during the M0 bootstrap'); N.3 ('only the bridge and the notifier inside the bridge package' call Telegram); N.5 'Secrets at rest' ('The bridge never opens ~/.config/dgist-agents/ except for the one-variable copy at bootstrap' plus a grep test of bridge/) vs N.5 'Conflicts and outages' and N.11 (the bridge sends Gmail with the DGIST agents' SMTP credentials, read at runtime); N.9 step 6 (DGIST bot as the fallback before Gmail); R.2 watchdog (Gmail when the bridge is silent)
findings.problem: Several rules conflict. (1) The M0 send-only notifier lives in the bridge package (N.3), so it must read the DGIST bot token from ~/.config/dgist-agents/course/service.env. (2) The bridge must send Gmail using credentials read at runtime from ~/.config/dgist-agents/{menu,notice}/service.env. (3) Yet the bridge must never open that directory, and a test greps bridge/ for the path. (4) A.4 limits the DGIST bot to the M0 bootstrap, but N.9 makes it the fallback when the programme's own bot token is revoked, which means reading its token at runtime. (5) The watchdog also needs Gmail, yet shares no code with the controller.
findings.scenario: Codex satisfies the grep test by copying the Gmail app password into ~/.config/smatsprint/, which breaks 'never copied'. Or the Gmail fallback fails the test. Or three components each grow their own reader of the DGIST files.
findings.fix: N.5 'Secrets at rest', replace the sentence with: 'Exactly two files may name ~/.config/dgist-agents/. bridge/dgist_send.py reads TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN and TELEGRAM_OWNER_CHAT_ID from course/service.env at send time; it only calls sendMessage and is used in the M0 bootstrap and when the programme's bot token is revoked. ops/notify/gmail_send.py reads GMAIL_* from menu/ or notice/service.env at send time, read-only, and never copies them. The bridge, the watchdog and the controller call these as subprocesses. A tree-wide grep test allows the path in exactly these two files.' A.4: change 'during the M0 bootstrap' to 'during the M0 bootstrap and as the fallback when the programme's own bot token is revoked'.
findings.test: A grep over the tree finds 'dgist-agents' only in the two allowed files. The fake 'Telegram down for 30 minutes' test sends through gmail_send.py. A value scan finds no GMAIL_APP_PASSWORD or DGIST bot token value anywhere under ~/.config/smatsprint/ or in the repository.

findings.where: Part A.5 rule 5 (project cap 30 GB; min_free_gb 65; hard_floor_gb 55); 00_README 'Disk'; C.5 worker admission ('disk (free space above the floors of Part A.5 and 3x the job's checkpoint size)'); D.6 offer filter ('disk >= 60 GB'); D.8 ('disk within 5 GB of min_free_gb on either host'); H.2 and H.4 layer 5 (the sandbox has its own caches)
findings.problem: (a) With 80 GB free on 2026-09-23 and a 65 GB floor, only about 15 GB can be used before new work stops, not the 30 GB cap. Two independent uv caches plus venvs (torch and CUDA wheels take about 5-6 GB per cache), a Playwright browser, Warp, Triton and Inductor caches, and any external dataset could consume 12-15 GB before the first rollout. The README also notes that other users move the disk 'by tens of GB a day'. (b) The same floors applied on a Vast worker cannot be met: the offer filter allows a 60 GB disk, whose free space is always under 65 GB, so the worker never admits a job on Vast.
findings.scenario: In its first days the campaign stalls on disk_floor, from its own installs or a neighbour's growth, and asks the user for decisions the handoff could have settled. In M5, the first real job never starts on the rented instance.
findings.fix: A.5 rule 5, add: 'Floors are per host. The lab uses min_free_gb 65 and hard_floor_gb 55. A Vast worker uses min_free_gb = max(10, 3x the declared checkpoint and rollout size of its queued jobs) and hard_floor_gb 5, on its own disk. In D.8, "either host" means each host's own floors.' H.4 layer 5: 'The uv wheel cache is shared between the lanes (the sandbox gets hard links and a read-only bind). Separate caches apply to compiled and runtime caches: Warp, Triton, Inductor, __pycache__.' Phase 0 and M0: 'Measure the disk after the science venv is built. Send one decision need with the headroom above the 65 GB floor and the campaign's projected need for 14 days, and three options: free part of ugrp-neurips-2027/runs (README Question 5), lower min_free_gb to 62, or accept pauses.' B.6: 'Download only the subset of the offline-replay dataset that is needed (level walking at 0.6, 1.2 and 1.8 m/s; hip kinematics and moments), at most 2 GB.'
findings.test: A unit test of the admission rule, with host=vast and a 60 GB disk, admits a job when 30 GB are free. `du -sh` of the project and the sandbox after the M1 installs is recorded in docs/PLAN.md and is 10 GB or less. The disk decision need exists at M0 and carries measured numbers.

findings.where: 00_README Defaults 'Seeds' ('>= 10 for any "equivalent to SMAT" claim'); Part G.2 L4(b) (two one-sided tests against the reproduced SMAT, on at least 5 seeds); G.7 mechanism path ('within +/-2 percentage points by two one-sided tests on 5 seeds'); page one ('Where they differ from this prompt, the README wins'); B.7 Q6 ('Seeds to 5')
findings.problem: An equivalence claim against SMAT needs at least 10 seeds according to the README, but 5 according to the gate text. The README wins over the prompt, so Codex must decide which number goes into gate/criteria.yaml at the M1 freeze. The campaign also only ever reaches 5 seeds (Q6).
findings.scenario: Codex freezes 5, and the README's stricter rule is silently dropped. Or it freezes 10, and the mechanism path (the most likely paper) needs about 5 more full pipelines plus controls, which no block budgets (about 3 B transitions).
findings.fix: Choose one number and write it everywhere. Recommended text for G.2 L4(b), G.7 and the README: 'Equivalence and non-inferiority claims (L4b, the mechanism path's two one-sided tests, B.5 learning parity) use at least 10 independent seeds; superiority claims use at least 5.' Add a block Q6b: 'Seeds to 10 for the SMAT arm and the best matched velocity controller (about 3 B).' Add to page one: 'Gate numbers live only in Part G; the README quotes them and does not override them.'
findings.test: gate/criteria.yaml contains min_seeds.equivalence = 10 and min_seeds.superiority = 5. In the synthetic-ledger suite, an equivalence claim with 5 seeds fails alone. campaign.yaml contains Q6b.

findings.where: Part B.2 Observations (Stage 4 'gains the two current normalised exo commands'), Episodes (0.2 rad tracking termination), B.3 registry; G.2 L1 ('falls in at most 10 %'); G.3 (no definition of 'fall'); C.9 walk_eval; C.5 checkpoint contents
findings.problem: Codex would have to guess items that change results. (1) smat_spec.json records a timing ambiguity: the 'current' exo torque in the Stage-4 human input may be this step's command (the exo acts first) or the last applied one. B.2 does not register the choice. (2) Does the 0.2 rad tracking termination still apply to hip DOFs whose imitation is released in S3-S4? If so, the human cannot move its hip more than about 11 degrees off the reference, which caps the very effect being studied. (3) The prompt defines neither 'fall' nor whether tracking termination is active during evaluation; MyoAssist's evaluator switches it off. (4) Should MyoAssist's runtime model edits be reproduced: a 14.81 degree torso pitch written into body_quat, and 30 settling steps at 50 % excitation (myoassist_facts setup_sequence)? (5) C.5's checkpoint list omits the per-env observation history (the exo actor's three-sample buffers), the reward memory (previous activation, previous command for the torque-rate penalty) and the torch RNG. (6) When the Stage-4 human input grows by 2, the prompt does not say that the critic input and the observation normaliser grow with it.
findings.scenario: Defaults get hard-coded without a registry entry. A key difference from SMAT becomes invisible and cannot be swept. The resume bit-equality test fails, and Codex debugs it by trial and error.
findings.fix: B.3, add rows: 'stage4_exo_input_timing: last applied u_{t-1} (default) | this step's exo command (exo acts first)'; 'tracking_termination_joints: tracked joints minus the DOFs whose imitation is released in this stage (default) | all tracked joints'; 'myoassist_runtime_edits: none (default) | MyoAssist torso pitch and 30 settling steps'. G.3: 'A fall is pelvis_ty < 0.70 m. Evaluation runs with tracking termination off and ends only at a fall or at 12 s; the fall rate is falls / E.' C.5: add 'per-env observation history buffers, reward memory, the torch and CUDA RNG states' to the checkpoint contents. B.2 Stage 4: 'the critic input and the observation normaliser grow by the same 2 inputs, under the same initialisation rule.'
findings.test: The registry schema test lists the new ids with their defaults. A walk_eval unit test on a scripted rollout that deviates 0.3 rad at the hip without falling counts no fall. The resume bit-equality test passes on a job interrupted at an update boundary in the middle of an episode.

findings.where: Part B.7 rows Q5 and Q6; B.6 intro ('lets the human co-adapt ... for the same 66 M transitions unless it says otherwise'), B1 ('human co-adapted'), B3 (6 variants); B.6 cross-play and G.5 partner seeds 900-949; C.10 'Model identity'; B.7 Q2 (sweeps registry choice 8, the timestep)
findings.problem: Q5 calls 'A1, B1 and B3' cheap, but B.6 makes B1 co-adapted at 66 M, and B3's 6 variants inherit the 66 M default. That puts Q5 at about 2.8 B instead of 1.4 B, and Q6 with its controls at about 2.3 B or more instead of 1.4 B. The held-out partner humans (seeds 900-949) that cross-play needs are trained in no block. C.10 refuses comparisons across timesteps, yet Q2's selection rule ranks members that differ in timestep.
findings.scenario: Codex either freezes the human for B1 and B3, against B.6, or silently doubles Q5's time. Q6's cross-play has no partners to play with. The model-identity check refuses Q2's own selection.
findings.fix: B.6: 'B1 and the B3 variants are screened with the S2 human frozen (2 M transitions each). B1 and the declared best B3 variant are then co-adapted for 66 M.' B.7: Q5 row '~2.0 B, ~28 h'; Q6 row '~2.3 B'; add a row 'Q6p: held-out partner humans, 3 seeds from 900-949 (S1-S2 each), ~1.4 B'. C.10, add: 'The model-identity rule applies to the arms of a claim. Members of one sweep may differ in any registered choice, timestep included.'
findings.test: The summed budgets in campaign.yaml match the B.7 table to within 10 %. A Q2 selection over mixed timesteps runs. A claim whose arms differ in timestep is refused.

findings.where: Part D.3 ('Every git push goes through one function ... with a minimum spacing of 30 s' vs status 'command-state, phase and transition-progress changes publish at once, at most one push per 5 s'); C.4 step 4 ('commit ledger/ and docs/ from state/trees/ledger/ on the ledger branch') vs C.2 (ledger/ and docs/ in the main tree; Codex edits docs/); D.1 and A.5 rule 5 (the 90 s pause target; no controller poll interval for control)
findings.problem: The single push function enforces 30 s spacing, yet a pause acknowledgement must publish 'at once'. docs/ is written on two branches by two writers: the runner on the ledger branch and Codex on main. ledger/ appears both in main's layout and in a worktree of the ledger branch. The interval at which the controller fetches the control branch is never stated, although the 90 s button-to-free target depends on it.
findings.scenario: The phone shows PAUSED 30 s or more after the GPU was freed, so the M2 acceptance line (120 s) is flaky. Weekly notes and PROGRESS.md diverge across branches, and fast-forward pushes fail.
findings.fix: D.3: 'The push function spaces pushes per ref: status at least 5 s apart (command and phase changes go immediately), main and ledger at least 60 s apart. The controller fetches control every 10 s.' C.2 and C.4: 'ledger/ and the runner-written documents (docs/generated/weekly/, docs/generated/paper/, docs/generated/REPRO.md) exist only on the ledger branch (worktree state/trees/ledger/). The docs/ tree on main (PLAN, PROGRESS, HANDOFF, USER_ACTIONS, spec/, HOP_IN_HOP_OUT) is written only by Codex sessions.'
findings.test: Fake-git test: a pause acknowledged at t=0 is pushed to status by t+6 s even though a main push happened at t-10 s. Tests assert that the runner writes nothing outside ledger/ and docs/generated/, and that Codex sessions write nothing inside them.

findings.where: Part N.9 step 4 ('push the skeleton'); N.7 (gh auth login with --git-protocol ssh --skip-ssh-key); D.3 'Controller auth' and 'Threat model' (ruleset A with the deploy key as the only bypass actor; 'verify against current docs'); fact gh-16
findings.problem: At step 4 no push credential exists. The build's gh login deliberately uploads no SSH key, and the deploy key is described only under D.3 and M2. Codex may improvise with `gh auth setup-git`, which writes a credential helper into the shared ~/.gitconfig, or by uploading an account SSH key. The ruleset design depends on a deploy key as bypass actor, which the verified fact gh-16 found undocumented for branch rulesets, and the prompt gives no fallback if the API rejects it.
findings.scenario: Codex edits shared git or SSH configuration that the forge also uses. Or M2 stalls when the ruleset API rejects the bypass actor, and Codex silently weakens the rulesets or drops them.
findings.fix: N.9 step 4: 'Create ~/.config/smatsprint/deploy_key (ed25519, mode 0600), add it with `gh repo deploy-key add --allow-write`, set core.sshCommand in the repository's own .git/config to `ssh -i ~/.config/smatsprint/deploy_key -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -o UserKnownHostsFile=~/.config/smatsprint/known_hosts`, then push. Never run gh auth setup-git, never upload an account SSH key, never edit ~/.gitconfig or ~/.ssh/config.' D.3: 'Create ruleset A with bypass actor type DeployKey. If the API rejects it, protect gh-pages only, with no bypass (the shell is then updated during M2 by disabling the ruleset with the build's gh session). Leave main, ledger and status writable, and show on the dashboard: "A leaked dashboard token can alter the GitHub copies; the lab copy is the source of truth."'
findings.test: After M0, `git config --global --list` and ~/.ssh/config are byte-identical to their Phase-0 snapshots. The real-token ruleset tests of D.3 pass, or the fallback banner is shown and a PUT to gh-pages is refused.

findings.where: Part H.4 layer 1 (the jail binds nothing of the experiment tree; 'sandbox copy' is a jailed process; --tmpfs $HOME; --dev-bind /dev/nvidia*); H.7 copy-in; H.8 ('code written in the sandbox')
findings.problem: copy-in must read experiment configs and checkpoints, but it is listed as a jailed process, in a jail that binds nothing of the experiment tree. --tmpfs $HOME hides the uv-managed interpreter under ~/.local/share/uv/python that a venv may point to. /dev/nvidia* is a shell glob, not a bwrap argument, and NVML and EGL may also need /proc, /dev/dri and parts of /sys. Nothing says how code gets into the sandbox tree, yet H.8 speaks of 'code written in the sandbox'.
findings.scenario: copy-in fails inside the jail, or Codex binds experiment directories into the jail read-only and weakens LI7 and the LI9 allow-list. The jailed viewer fails with 'python: not found' or 'CUDA driver not found'.
findings.fix: H.4 layer 1: remove 'sandbox copy' from the list of jailed processes, and add: 'sprintctl sbx copy-in runs outside the jail, in smatsprint-ctl.slice. It reads the experiment, writes only the sandbox's copies/ directory, and enforces the held-out allow-list. The jail ro-binds the installation of `readlink -f <sandbox venv>/bin/python`, uses --proc /proc and --dev /dev, then adds --dev-bind for each existing /dev/nvidia* and /dev/dri/* node, enumerated in Python. It sets HOME, TMPDIR, XDG_CACHE_HOME, WARP_CACHE_PATH, TRITON_CACHE_DIR and TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR inside the sandbox tree. Sandbox code is a `git archive <commit> smatsprint eval` into the sandbox tree, made by `sprintctl sbx code sync [<commit>]`.'
findings.test: Inside the jail: `python -c 'import torch; torch.ones(1).cuda()'`, nvidia-smi and an EGL render all succeed, and `ls /home/aurnab/projects/smat-sprint` fails. copy-in of a held-out partner checkpoint is refused; copy-in of an S2 checkpoint is accepted.

findings.where: Part H.10 'Tested, not trusted' ('Each powershell block is linted against the PowerShell 5.1 rules above and its ssh command line is executed from Linux as the equivalent call'); E.2 Guide group; A.5 rule 5 (nothing under /tmp)
findings.problem: The sail-gpu alias exists only in the PC's ~/.ssh/config. On the server, `ssh sail-gpu` would need a self-SSH key in the shared ~/.ssh, which the forge also uses. `ssh -N -L 8801:...` never returns. There is no pwsh or PSScriptAnalyzer on the server, so 'linted for PowerShell 5.1' has no tool behind it. And 'SMATSPRINT_HOME in a temp directory' conflicts with A.5's 'nothing under /tmp'.
findings.scenario: Codex adds a key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (shared state), or a test hangs on -N, or the lint is an empty stub that passes everything.
findings.fix: H.10, replace the powershell sentence with: 'Each powershell block is checked by tests/guide/ps51_lint.py, which rejects &&, ||, 2>/dev/null, POSIX paths and bash syntax and allows only a listed set of cmdlets and ssh. Its ssh line is parsed by a strict grammar (host sail-gpu; optionally -N and -L 8801:127.0.0.1:8801) and executed against a user-level sshd on 127.0.0.1:28022, with a throwaway host key and authorized_keys under cache/guide-sshd/, using `ssh -F cache/guide-sshd/ssh_config` that maps sail-gpu to it; ~/.ssh is not touched. Tunnels run under `timeout 20` and are verified by fetching the viewer through the forwarded port. Throwaway instances live under <project>/cache/guide/.'
findings.test: The guide suite passes, and ~/.ssh hashes the same before and after. A guide block containing && fails the lint. The tunnel test fetches the viewer page, with its token, through the forwarded port.

findings.where: Part B.2 'Reference motion' (short_reference_gait.npz); D.5 ('a unit test greps the resume path for ... allow_pickle=True'; 'anything that has been on a rented host is untrusted data when it returns'); D.2 (work/refdata/ travels with every move); fact myoassist reference_data ('each is a pickled dict stored as a 0-d object array')
findings.problem: Loading MyoAssist's reference file requires np.load(allow_pickle=True). D.5 limits the no-pickle grep to the resume path, so the environment's reference loader would unpickle files from work/refdata/, and work/refdata/ travels to Vast and back. D.5 says data returning from a rented host is untrusted.
findings.scenario: A hostile or corrupted Vast host replaces a refdata file. At the next load on the lab, the unpickle executes code, unless the loader happens to verify the hash before calling np.load.
findings.fix: B.2, add: 'In M1, tools/convert_reference.py (the only file allowed to call allow_pickle=True) verifies the sha256 of the MyoAssist file, then writes ref_<sha>.npz holding plain float64 arrays plus a JSON header. Every runtime loader uses np.load(allow_pickle=False) and checks the converted file's sha256 before loading. The no-pickle grep covers smatsprint/, eval/, runner/ and control/, with that one exemption.'
findings.test: A grep finds allow_pickle=True only in tools/convert_reference.py. The loader refuses an npz that contains an object array. The converted reference reproduces the original arrays exactly.

findings.where: Part E.4 Phase 0 probes; E.5 ('Playwright's browser download' counted as user space; 'Expected: none'); E.2 Dashboard group (Playwright); H.4 (bwrap with CUDA); C.12 (EGL clips); 00_README 'PC-only' list
findings.problem: Headless Chromium needs system libraries, which `playwright install-deps` installs with sudo. EGL rendering and a jailed CUDA context can also fail for system reasons. Phase 0 probes EGL and bwrap but says nothing about what to do when a probe fails, and Playwright is not probed until M2. Each late discovery becomes its own PC-only root trip.
findings.scenario: M2's Playwright suite fails on missing system libraries such as libnss3 or libatk. The dashboard cannot pass its gate, and a root need reaches the user days after the one moment they were at the PC.
findings.fix: E.4 Phase 0, add: 'Run one detached prerequisite probe: a Playwright headless Chromium launch (browsers under <project>/cache/ms-playwright), an EGL render of the exported model, a jailed torch CUDA matmul, and `loginctl show-user aurnab -p Linger`. Bundle every failure into one ops/root/<date>-prereqs.sh and one PC-only need, sent during M0 while the user is expected to still be near the PC. Fallbacks: OSMesa for clips (slower, labelled as such); Playwright's Firefox if Chromium's libraries are missing.'
findings.test: docs/PLAN.md lists the four probe results. If any probe failed, exactly one root_needed need exists, and it was created during M0.

findings.where: Part N.8 session command and 'standard continue prompt'; A.4 ('uv ... not on the PATH of non-interactive shells or units'); E.9 ('the user answers through needs or by editing the README'; the spec is copied once into docs/spec/)
findings.problem: Wrapper sessions are systemd transient units, so their PATH contains neither ~/.local/bin nor sprintctl, yet the continue prompt says 'create needs with sprintctl need create'. The spec is copied into docs/spec/ once, while the README invites the user to answer by editing the README, or parts/ plus assemble.py, in the handoff folder, which later sessions never re-read. The account's Codex quota is shared with the forge's builder, which is in its own M1 at the same time, and nothing bounds this programme's session rate.
findings.scenario: The first wrapper session fails on 'sprintctl: command not found' or improvises paths. A later answer the user writes in the handoff README is ignored. Back-to-back 10 h xhigh sessions exhaust the shared quota and stall the forge's build.
findings.fix: N.8: 'The wrapper launches sessions with --setenv=PATH=/home/aurnab/.local/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin (sprintctl is installed as ~/.local/bin/sprintctl, a symlink into the service tree) and --setenv=SMATSPRINT_HOME=<abs path>, with GH_TOKEN and GITHUB_TOKEN unset. It launches at most build_sessions_per_day sessions (default 3).' Continue prompt, add as the first line: 'Diff /home/aurnab/projects/smat-sprint-autoresearch-handoff/{00_README.md,CODEX_MASTER_PROMPT.md,02_RESEARCH_DIRECTIONS.md} against docs/spec/. If they changed, copy and commit them, and list the changes first in your report.'
findings.test: A fake-codex session unit runs `command -v sprintctl uv gh` successfully. Editing the handoff README produces a docs/spec commit in the next session. The wrapper refuses a fourth launch within 24 h at the default setting.

findings.problem: The prompt has wrong or dangling references, undefined terms and colliding names. (1) H.5 'Add seeds ... pre-drawn training-seed pool (Part C.10)': the pools are in C.3. (2) H.2 and H.5 'host limits (ceilings) of Part A.5': these are in limits.toml (D.3). (3) C.9 sprint protocol '(Part G.6)': should be G.2 L5 and G.3. (4) H.9 '(Part A.4)': author contact is only in the README. (5) D.2 evacuate '(c) the disposable list of D.7' and invariant I3 authorise deletion from a list that D.7 never defines. (6) 'optional Mode B' (E.4 M7) is defined nowhere. (7) 'the forge's D.4', 'the forge's D.7' and 'as in the forge' (D.4 fixed texts, D.5, E.2 model and chaos tests) point to no server path for the forge's handoff document. (8) 'the KB's program document' and 'METHODS-AND-BACKENDS.md' (B.6 K1-K3; B.8's phase-adaptive delay-compensated profile and optimised biological-moment mapping) are not on the server. (9) P1-P3 name the positive controls (B.6) and also the proxy tiers (C.7), in adjacent rows: Q1 'positive control P1' and Q2 'at P1 = 40 M'. G1-G5 and G.1-G.5, C0-C9 and C.1-C.14, B0-B5 and B.1-B.10 also collide, less dangerously.
findings.scenario: Codex invents a disposable list that deletes something I3 should protect, looks for a Mode B that does not exist, cannot find the forge texts it is told to reuse, and mixes up tier P1 and positive control P1 in campaign.yaml ids.
findings.fix: Apply these edits. H.5 'Part C.10' -> 'Part C.3'. H.2 and H.5 'Part A.5' -> 'Part D.3 limits.toml'. C.9 '(Part G.6)' -> '(Part G.2 L5, G.3)'. H.9 '(Part A.4)' -> '(00_README, Question 2)'. D.7, add: 'Disposable list (shown with sizes; each item needs the user's typed confirmation): eval rollouts and clips of candidates below L1; logs older than 30 days; superseded run-tree venvs.' E.4 M7: delete 'and optional Mode B', or define it. A.4, add the server path of the forge's handoff folder (verify it in Phase 0, read-only), with 'where this prompt says "as in the forge", reuse the text from there with attribution'. B.8: define the two extra profiles in one sentence each, or delete them. Rename the positive controls PC1-PC3 everywhere, including campaign ids.
findings.test: tools/check_prompt.py gains a reference check: every 'Part X.n' resolves to a heading whose subject matches; 'disposable list' and 'Mode B' each resolve to a definition. campaign.yaml ids use the PC prefix for positive controls, and no id collides with a tier name.

strengths: Environment facts are verified, dated and sourced: host, delegated cgroup controllers, lingering, tool paths, free ports, and the forge's units, slices and floors. The prompt gives Codex absolute paths, and the rules for coexisting with the forge are explicit.

Part N is close to implementable as written: a typed need record, fixed check and reissue registries (never shell text from a message), template-only messages, and a fake Bot API test list. It is grounded in verified Telegram behaviour: the 409 conflict, the random reset of update ids after a week, 24 h retention, the 64-byte callback_data limit, and link_preview_options.
gh isolation (GH_CONFIG_DIR plus --insecure-storage, a pinned gh version, never revoking the OAuth app) is correctly derived from facts gh-05, gh-07 and gh-08.
Writing desired.json before any signal, epoch fencing, and a pure (state, event) state machine tested with fakes let the control plane be tested completely before any money or data is at risk.

The campaign is mechanically executable: paired blocks, equal-budget refusals, symbolic parents resolved by declared rules, job identity by code_id rather than commit, and registered selection rules. Codex does not have to invent research logic.

The MyoAssist defects (target-speed randomiser, dirty 3D resets, shared log-std, orphaned optimiser tensors) are cited with file and line numbers and turned into concrete environment tests (target speed exactly 1.25 m/s, every DOF reset, exactly 18 exo inputs).

The probe numbers are specific and actionable: MULTICCD disabled on both backends, 153 MB per process from .mjb against 560 MB from XML, measured per-process scaling and Warp memory per world. The parity gates rightly reject trajectory parity in favour of contact-free and statistical parity.

E.4's waiting rules (at most one 10-minute blocking call, detach.sh as a transient unit, notify once) and the anti-pattern list directly target the known failure modes: goal mode, narrating transfers, audits instead of runs.

The dashboard never re-implements a precondition: buttons, their enabled state and dialog numbers come from actions[] computed by the tested state machine. That removes a whole class of drift between the UI and the logic.
Checkpoints are never pickles (safetensors plus JSON), and mj_getState(mjSTATE_INTEGRATION) gives an exact, testable resume target.

Gate bands are fixed in the text before any result, with the reasoning behind their widths (G.4), and there are three paper paths. Together these stop both band-moving and the novelty-kill failure recorded in A.2.
